author: Jan Rey T. Obguia
title: "I don't condemn them because I know how they feel" - Byron Scott sparked backlash with his comments on the 1992 L.A. riots - NewsBreak
text:
By Jan Rey T. Obguia ,
1 days ago
Horrible things happen all the time, but the 1992 Los Angeles riots were right up there among the most devastating things to happen short of a war.
The resulting violence, triggered by the acquittal of four police officers filmed beating Rodney King, left 55 people dead and $1 billion worth of property damaged.
The unrest also puts the Los Angeles Lakers players in a precarious position. They were part of the city they call home, watching the same events unfold like everybody else.
Byron Scott , a Los Angeles native, was in an even deeper predicament. When the long-time Purple and Gold guard spoke about the riots, it triggered a wave of criticism and raised questions about where he stood on the violence.
Was B-Scott condoning the rioters? Scott grew up in South Central L.A. around 104th Street and Crenshaw. The riots happened right in his backyard, right in his own community.
At the time, April 29, 1992, to be exact, the Lakers were in the middle of a first-round playoff matchup with the Portland Trail Blazers. It was Game 3, and L.A.’s collective backs were practically against the wall. They won their only game of the series, 121-119 in overtime.
Scott had a fine outing. He scored 22, with four rebounds, four assists and two steals. But knowing what’s happening 12 miles outside The Forum weighed heavily on him. It was a minor miracle he finished the game, but his emotions couldn’t be contained right after.
“I’m upset by the verdict,” Scott said . “I thought it was pretty obvious what (the acquitted police officers) did was unjustified. Then again, it’s been happening here in L.A. for so many years, it’s no surprise to me. This is no different, except this time they were caught on videotape. And it still didn’t seem to make much difference.”
When asked whether he disapproved of the rioters, his answer was not what people expected.
“No, I don’t condemn them because I know how they feel. I wish they’d show their anger in a different direction, but people are going to be people and they’re going to show the way they feel one way or another. You know, I don’t condemn what they’re doing. I understand exactly what they’re doing. I understand why they’re doing it and I can’t condemn that,” added the three-time NBA champion.
Facing the backlash Scott immediately faced intense criticism for his comments. Worse, most of the outcry came from his L.A. neighbors. Even after helping the local sports team reach the league’s pinnacle over the past decade, they couldn’t cut the guy some slack for what he uttered in the heat of the moment.
“Condemn. I think that was the word I used that set people off. What I said was that I couldn’t condemn what the rioters were doing. What I meant was that I don’t condemn people. That I don’t judge them,” Scott clarified . “I’m sorry if it came out wrong. Don’t forget, I was pretty upset. That was my city out there that was burning. I was upset about the verdict, same way a lot of people were.”
“I understood why so many people were so angry. But I never, ever meant to suggest that I approved of what they were doing, that it was justified. What they did was horrible. It made me sick,” he added.
April 29 was a Wednesday, but Scott couldn’t have imagined how things would escalate over the weekend. He soon found himself under fire on radio talk shows and in the letter sections of newspapers. Critics accused him of encouraging further violence and abusing his platform as a public figure.
Scott admitted he was hurt, but he also feared for his life and his loved ones’.
“The one that really got to me was a letter from some guy who said something about, ‘Next time you guys choke in the playoffs, maybe we’ll come over to your house and burn it down and you’ll understand how we feel.’ That, to me, is totally ignorant. He’s talking about hurting my family, my children, my home,” B-Scott stated. “That’s when I realized that it was important for me to try to clarify what I said.”
Some things never change The Los Angeles riots happened over 34 years ago, but the issues that fueled the unrest continue to surface around the world. From anger over police brutality to frustration with governments and public institutions, people still take to the streets when they feel ignored.
Sometimes, these demonstrations remain peaceful. On other occasions, they descend into violence, as France recently witnessed.
The circumstances may differ, but the questions remain the same. How do people respond when they believe justice has failed them? Where does understanding their anger end and excusing violence begin?
In 1992, Scott found himself sandwiched between the two sides. He said he understood their reaction, but people interpreted his words negatively. Sometimes, trying to please everyone leaves you with no one and that’s the saddest part.
